title: San Juan County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: San Juan County wells have a 100 ft median depth. Compare reported yields, $12,500-$22,000 finished-well costs, mine-related risks and permit records.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in San Juan County
intro_html:
A well budget in San Juan County starts with the rock beneath the lot, not just the county average. Reported wells have a median depth of 100 feet, but mountain bedrock can produce very different results on neighboring properties.

Colorado DWR records contain 243 permitted wells countywide, with 89 recorded as constructed. Depth, yield and water-level information is available for smaller groups. Use these figures as a starting point around Silverton and elsewhere in the county, then check the actual completion records closest to the property.

sections.heading: A 100-Foot Median, With Room for Deeper Drilling
sections.html:
Among the 92 wells reporting depth, the median is 100 feet and the middle half runs 58-200 feet. That is a useful starting range for a bid, not a target depth the driller can promise. The 90th-percentile depth is 319 feet, and the deepest reported well reaches 480 feet.

Most permit aquifer entries are unnamed or identified as fractured bedrock. In that setting, usable water depends on intersecting connected fractures; drilling deeper does not automatically mean getting more water. Ask for a bid that explains how additional footage and casing are charged. Around Silverton, compare nearby completion logs and terrain before applying the county median to a particular lot.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Look Useful, but the Sample Is Small
sections.html:
Only 24 wells report a pump yield. Their median is 11.0 gpm, with the middle half between 7.4 and 15.0 gpm. Those reported rates are encouraging for household planning, but a completion-test yield is not a guarantee of sustained production through changing conditions.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 12% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. That does not establish that low-producing or unsuccessful wells are absent from the county. For a purchase, have the existing well tested for sustained output and recovery. Match that result to household demand, pump equipment and any storage needs rather than relying on the county yield alone.

sections.heading: Water May Stand Above the Bottom of the Borehole
sections.html:
The 16 static-water-level reports show a median depth to water of 40 feet, with the middle half at 7-52 feet. Static level is where water stands when the well is resting. It is not the total drilled depth, and it does not tell you how far the level will fall while pumping.

These records do not establish a rising or falling water-table trend. There is no time series here for making that call, and fractured-bedrock wells may tap different water-bearing zones. For an existing San Juan County well, ask for dated measurements and a pumping test. A resting water level alone cannot establish dependable supply or the right pump setting.

sections.heading: San Juan County’s Permit History Needs Careful Reading
sections.html:
Permit issuance spans decades: 7 in the 1970s, 51 in the 1980s, 29 in the 1990s, 33 in the 2000s, 49 in the 2010s and 47 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so the latest decade is incomplete. These are permits, not a count of finished household wells; 36% of the use mix is domestic/household and 31% is monitoring.

The most active driller-field entries include Dak Drilling Llc (Rathjen, Doug) and Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.), with 10 each. The label “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” appears on 35 records; treat that as a record label, not a verified drilling-company name. Historical activity does not establish current availability.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole Near Silverton
sections.html:
The county cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, described as granite/gneiss, at $65-$100 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $6,500-$10,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $12,500-$22,000.

Use that as a planning allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. The 58-200-foot middle depth range leaves substantial uncertainty in footage alone. Have the contractor separate drilling, casing and grout from pump installation and service connections. Mountain access, rig setup and the route between the well and house need a site review. Confirm what the quote includes before comparing bids, especially where excavation or electrical work is priced separately.

sections.heading: Mine Features and Cleanup Sites Warrant a Water Check
sections.html:
The supplied environmental mapping lists 9,581 historic mine features, 33 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 14 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles. These are screening flags, not evidence that a particular well is contaminated. A sampling location also does not necessarily represent a confirmed contamination finding.

Before buying, review nearby site records and arrange laboratory testing suited to drinking water and local mining concerns. Discuss metals and any relevant PFAS testing with the laboratory or health authority. Separately, inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage, and check the septic layout. The permit dataset does not establish a dry-hole rate, so do not interpret an unconstructed or incomplete record as a failed borehole.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a San Juan County Lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s DWR permit and completion record, not just the seller’s description of a “domestic well.” Confirm the authorized uses, well location and any permit conditions. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize outdoor watering. Where applicable, water-right or augmentation requirements need review before you commit to a use.

Then compare nearby wells around Silverton and the property itself. A countywide average is not interchangeable with records from Ouray County or San Miguel County. For a new build, lay out the well, septic system, house, driveway and utility trenches together, with required separations confirmed locally. Keep drilling access available and make water-supply verification part of the purchase decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in San Juan County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 100 feet, and the middle half of wells is 58-200 feet deep. These figures come from 92 depth reports. The deepest recorded well is 480 feet. Fractured-bedrock conditions make nearby completion logs more useful for a specific lot than the county median by itself.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in San Juan County?
faq.a: The supplied model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 100-foot median depth, the hole costs about $6,500-$10,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $12,500-$22,000. Get a site-specific quote that spells out access, casing, additional footage and connection work.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in San Juan County?
faq.a: Among 24 reported pump yields, the median is 11.0 gpm and the middle half is 7.4-15.0 gpm. The reported 1-5 gpm share is 12%. Those results cannot guarantee production on another lot. For an existing home, test sustained output and recovery before deciding whether the supply meets your needs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in San Juan County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through testing and inspection. Nearby mapping includes 9,581 historic mine features, 33 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 14 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles. Proximity alone does not prove contamination. Review local site records and ask a laboratory about drinking-water testing, metals and relevant PFAS concerns.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in San Juan County?
faq.a: The supplied records do not show a water-table trend. Only 16 wells report static levels, with a median depth to water of 40 feet and a middle half of 7-52 feet. These measurements are not a time series. Dated measurements from the same well are needed to assess changes meaningfully.
